query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Above ~900 °C, if sufficient Al is present in CrFeCoNiX alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al), a stable, adherent, and slow-growing Al2O3-based scale forms, mitigating volatile Cr-oxide formation and reducing scale stress, which thereby prevents or substantially delays cracking and spallation; in contrast, when Al content is insufficient—or if Mn or Si dominates—multiphase oxides grow faster, build excessive stress, and spall.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) alloys in either single-phase or multiphase solid-solution states, all with similar thermomechanical histories and initial surface finish, prepared for high-temperature exposure in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres.
generation.intervention: Vary Al content in CrFeCoNiX systematically to examine the formation and adhesion of oxide scales above 900 °C, in controlled gaseous environments with in-situ analysis (e.g., TGA, XRD, TEM/EDS).
generation.conditions: Long-duration (~tens of hours) exposures at temperatures ≥900 °C with oxidizing or corrosive gases (e.g., air, O2-N2 mixtures), monitoring scale evolution real-time (if in-situ) or through staged ex-situ analyses.
generation.structural_mediator: Selective outward diffusion of Al (and Cr) at elevated temperatures forms dense, coherent oxide layers (Al2O3 or Cr2O3), altering growth kinetics and mechanical integrity of the scale.
generation.mechanism: Sufficient Al content drives the thermodynamics and kinetics towards a dense α-Al2O3 layer, which is slow-growing, resists volatility, and lowers stress buildup. If Al is too low or replaced by Mn or Si, the oxide scales become multi-layered, grow more quickly, and accumulate tensile stresses that lead to cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with ≥5–8 at.% Al will demonstrate stable, oxide scales with minimal spallation; lower or no Al additions (or primarily Mn, Si doping) will instead yield thick, multi-phase oxide layers susceptible to crack formation and scale loss.
generation.baseline: A reference CrFeCoNi composition without Al or only trace Al, tested under the same conditions, to compare scale morphology, growth kinetics, and spallation tendencies.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys with modest Al (up to ~10–12 at.%) or Mn/Si content, for isothermal exposures above 900 °C in air or similar oxidizing/corrosive environments of comparable severity.
generation.uncertainty: If Al additions fail to create a coherent oxide scale or if the presence of Mn or Si unexpectedly stabilizes a protective layer to the same extent, the proposed Al-based oxidation mechanism may need re-evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX alloys with incrementally varying Al (0 to ~10 at.%) while holding other elemental compositions constant. Subject them to identical high-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidizing treatments in controlled atmospheres. Characterize oxide growth kinetics using in-situ thermogravimetric analysis and perform cross-sectional TEM/EDS to ascertain compositional and structural details of the scale.
measurements: Phase composition via XRD to detect Al2O3 vs. other complex oxides.
Microstructural analyses (SEM/TEM) to quantify oxide thickness, morphology, and interface quality.
Spallation or cracking onset via visual inspection and acoustic emission monitoring.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Observation of significant oxide cracking, spallation, or non-Al2O3 scale formation in alloys with elevated Al content (≥5–8 at.%) would refute the claim that adequate Al promotes a stable, coherent, slow-growing oxide layer.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, CrMnFeCoNi HEA behaviour responding to changes in temperature and environmental factors such as the partial pressure of oxygen has been investigated by in situ XRD at high temperatures up to 1100 °C. In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. The presence of Mn, known for its high mobility and low-energy oxide formation, can deplete Mn in the alloy, causing pore formation and accelerating oxide growth. Tradition

Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures.
